name: Pare-Bench
intro: Pare-Bench 是 PARE 主动助手研究环境中的评测基准，包含 143 个跨通信、生产力、日程和生活应用的多样任务。PARE 将移动应用建模为有限状态机，并通过主动用户仿真构造情境，使 proactive assistant 必须观察用户行为、推断目标、判断干预时机并跨应用执行任务。
org: University of California, Santa Barbara; Apple; University of Washington; Independent Researcher
build_method: 有限状态机应用建模, 四阶段Agent场景生成, Oracle重试, 人工语义核验
metric: Success@4, Success^4, Success Rate, Proposal Rate, Acceptance Rate, 平均只读动作数
task_type: 主动助手任务, Agent任务, 多应用编排
eval_feature: 主动性, 状态依赖用户仿真, 扁平助手API, Oracle校验, 工具失败与噪声通知
task_type_en: Proactive assistant task, Agent task, Multi-app orchestration
build_method_en: Finite-state app modeling, four-stage agent scenario generation, oracle retries, human semantic review
eval_feature_en: Proactivity, state-dependent user simulation, flat assistant APIs, oracle validation, tool failures and noise notifications
intro_en: Pare-Bench is the benchmark built on the PARE proactive assistant research environment. It contains 143 diverse tasks across communication, productivity, scheduling, and lifestyle apps. PARE models mobile applications as finite state machines and uses active user simulation, forcing proactive assistants to observe user behavior, infer goals, decide when to intervene, and execute tasks across apps.
metric_en: Success@4, Success^4, Success Rate, Proposal Rate, Acceptance Rate, Average Read Actions

drawio_review_note: reviewed_at=2026-07-22; scope=source-stage paper-level Build Process reconstruction for Pare-Bench; primary-paper-pin=https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00842v1 and https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.00842v1; paper-v1-pdf-sha256=259caaeaa7d3cc16e232851469c6a1578ca7138cc7c89ec12ec961b9baf697d4; official-code-and-data-pin=https://github.com/deepakn97/pare/tree/261149914a9e9dcacb12de620575c691d50e3c2e; fixed-git-tar-sha256=c0c5aa90099adf7e397fb9f30b57f59d045aa0e35e5724c1d21847b21755c10e. The paper is the primary source for the scenario-construction method. The fixed Git snapshot verifies the currently released scenario files, split, runtime, and metric implementation; it is not treated as proof that every current code line was used for the paper's original candidate-generation run. The official paper and README do not link a separate Hugging Face dataset. The README's Hugging Face token instruction is for gated model access, not a dataset source, so no HF dataset revision or hash is invented. Independent fixed-snapshot evidence includes README sha256=25d73658f68ada88f4d390b6f3c319f52b427cb8d169e678cd97261e86d12a1a; LICENSE sha256=451caefbcf9f6c116aceb1eb646c70fd293c7c0bc19241baba98e298b18f87c2; data/splits/full.txt sha256=50b6d79aae2f0ba33d945b5ec86b0e2fab632bee170aba8f175d957f0020a269; scenario_metadata.json sha256=c55a55f2b3286baf1372a5e4fd77c7efe52a4f714695757c7cdd721db8715f74; the null-safe aggregate manifest of relative benchmark scenario paths plus per-file SHA256 is fe0e751a1c2216d10708cc46d3e6326d3d295a73eebcdee7b4778f1dc60d87aa; the aggregate apps Python manifest is b66174d873d378daf12f16ace5a0fa8c3a17bd4a6289dc3a04959473179ac604; pare/benchmark/report_stats.py sha256=59b6b96fee9059ca2e5684ddc0ab189a5718c5bae8edeaa15b97292197644a00; and pare/scenario_runner.py sha256=73be3b3991422f325eb5e460b266f561fcb3dc03492e065938af18abae1cca92. The fixed full split contains 143 nonempty scenario names and the repository contains 143 Python scenario files under pare/scenarios/benchmark, giving a directly verified released count. scenario_metadata.json has only 20 entries and is therefore not used as the benchmark-count authority. Paper-v1 construction facts retained in both language specs are that PARE extends ARE with an active user simulator while preserving reusable apps, scenarios, verification, and shared persistent state. The paper's Table 5 scope is nine user-facing FSM applications across four domains plus System, Agent UI, and FileSystem as three core applications. Each user application models screens as states and navigation or forms as transitions while tracking current, active, and background application state. The user receives state-dependent tools; the assistant receives flat application APIs; both modify the same persistent environment. Each scenario has three components: initial application state and seeded data, an event flow containing environment and oracle actions, and final-state validation criteria. The four-stage generator is a code agent based on the Claude Agent SDK with read-only access to the Pare codebase and a required set of target applications. Stage 1 writes a natural-language story around a latent user goal and uses an LLM-as-a-judge uniqueness check against existing descriptions; a duplicate returns to Stage 1, while a unique story continues to app population. Stage 2 generates init_and_populate_apps. Stage 3 constructs the event flow with scheduled environment events plus oracle user and assistant actions. Stage 4 defines validation criteria and required completion actions. Each of Stages 2 through 4 executes oracle and environment events to catch syntax or execution errors; a failure returns execution feedback to the corresponding generating stage for retry, while all passing checks continue to human review. Paper section 5 explicitly states that the authors verify every candidate for story coherence, correctness of task-execution validation criteria, and realism of scenario-event content before finalizing 143 scenarios across communication, productivity, scheduling, and lifestyle domains; Appendix E abbreviates this as a human semantic-coherence check and does not negate the fuller section-5 rubric. No undocumented automatic acceptance threshold or undisclosed human-vote count is inferred. Two generator reproducibility boundaries are explicit. The paper says the generator is based on the Claude Agent SDK but does not disclose immutable generator or uniqueness-judge checkpoints. In addition, the paper names the Stage-3 function build_event_flow while fixed released scenario code uses build_events_flow. The diagram therefore preserves the paper name in the primary construction flow and records the fixed-code pluralized name only in a dashed boundary. The fixed snapshot may postdate the paper and cannot recover the unpublished candidate-generation history. The paper evaluation runs each scenario four times with a GPT-5-mini active user simulator, at most ten turns, one user iteration, five Observe iterations, and ten Execute iterations; the same assistant model is used for Observe and Execute. At each turn the user acts first with only current-state tools; accept_proposal and reject_proposal are available for a pending proposal, while Appendix B shows that the user may instead ignore it and gather context. Observe mode then receives the user action and full notifications but exposes read-only operations, wait, or propose. An accepted proposal enters Execute mode with the complete cross-application flat API and performs only the approved task; execution completion, rejection, or continued context gathering returns to the next user-first turn. Episode completion or maximum-turn truncation alone exits the loop to final-state oracle validation. Appendix B classifies proposal outcomes as accept, reject, gather context, and truncated, with gather-context trajectories later resolving to accept, reject, or truncation. The final oracle checks whether user goals are fulfilled and records proposals, acceptances, read-only actions, and turns. Robustness variants are evaluation configurations over the complete user-observe-interaction loop: independent tool-failure probabilities 0.1, 0.2, or 0.4 perturb transitions, while Poisson background noise at 2, 4, or 6 events per minute is interleaved with scenario events; neither is a proposal-decision prerequisite. Paper metrics are Success@k for at least one successful run, Success^k for all successful runs, ordinary success rate, proposal rate, acceptance rate, and average read-only actions. The fixed report_stats.py first filters null success_numeric rows, then renders Pass@k when any remaining run succeeds and Pass^k when every remaining valid run succeeds. Because k is derived from the unfiltered frame, a scenario with fewer than k valid runs can still satisfy fixed-code Pass^k; this is a denominator drift from the paper requirement that all k runs succeed, not merely a naming change. The fixed scenario_runner.py also stores read_only_actions as proactive-agent plus user-agent read-only calls, whereas the paper interprets Read Actions as a proxy for assistant information gathering. Both fixed-code semantic drifts are explicit in the metric boundary rather than normalized away. A separate app-count documentation drift is also preserved: paper Table 5 lists nine FSM plus three core applications, whereas the fixed README summarizes nine domain plus two core applications and omits FileSystem from that count. The graph follows the paper's methodological scope and records the README wording only as dashed evidence. The fixed release is MIT licensed. Primary edges encode the paper-backed construction, duplicate and oracle retry loops, user-first Observe/Execute loop, robustness configuration branch, and episode termination; dashed edges encode source pins, the undisclosed generator/checkpoints and function-name drift, app-count documentation drift, released-file verification, absence of an official HF dataset link, and fixed metric-semantics drift.
